cards.q: Which neurotransmitter does a somatic motor neuron release onto a skeletal muscle fiber?
cards.a: Acetylcholine.
options: Norepinephrine
Acetylcholine
Glutamate
Glycine
cards.explanation: Every somatic motor neuron in the body releases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, which is why one drug class can affect all voluntary muscle. Norepinephrine is the transmitter of most sympathetic postganglionic fibers onto smooth muscle and glands, not onto skeletal muscle. Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter inside the central nervous system, and glycine is an inhibitory transmitter in the spinal cord.

cards.q: When the action potential reaches the axon terminal, which ion enters the terminal and triggers vesicle fusion?
cards.a: Ca2+.
options: Ca2+
Na+
K+
Cl-
cards.explanation: Depolarization of the terminal opens voltage gated Ca2+ channels, and the Ca2+ that enters is the direct signal for synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release acetylcholine. Na+ entry carries the action potential along the axon but does not itself trigger release. K+ efflux repolarizes the terminal, and Cl- movement plays no role in the release step.

cards.q: What kind of receptor does acetylcholine bind on the motor end plate?
cards.a: A nicotinic cholinergic receptor that is itself an ion channel.
options: A beta adrenergic receptor coupled to adenylyl cyclase
A muscarinic cholinergic receptor coupled to a G protein
A nicotinic cholinergic receptor that is itself an ion channel
A ryanodine receptor in the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane
cards.explanation: The end plate receptor is nicotinic: the binding site and the channel pore are parts of the same protein, so the channel opens within a fraction of a millisecond of acetylcholine binding. Muscarinic receptors also bind acetylcholine but act through G proteins and are found on cardiac and smooth muscle and glands, not on the skeletal end plate. The ryanodine receptor sits on the sarcoplasmic reticulum and is opened later in the sequence, and beta adrenergic receptors bind catecholamines rather than acetylcholine.

cards.q: Which enzyme in the synaptic cleft breaks down acetylcholine?
cards.a: Acetylcholinesterase.
options: Monoamine oxidase
Acetylcholinesterase
Catechol O methyltransferase
Choline acetyltransferase
cards.explanation: Acetylcholinesterase is anchored in the basal lamina of the cleft and splits acetylcholine into choline and acetate within a couple of milliseconds, which is what allows the end plate to repolarize between action potentials. Choline acetyltransferase does the opposite job, building acetylcholine inside the terminal from choline and acetyl CoA. Monoamine oxidase and catechol O methyltransferase degrade catecholamines, not acetylcholine.

cards.q: What is an end plate potential?
cards.a: A graded depolarization produced by ligand gated channels.
options: A slow depolarization produced by a G protein coupled second messenger
An all or none depolarization produced by voltage gated Na+ channels
A graded hyperpolarization produced by ligand gated Cl- channels
A graded depolarization produced by ligand gated channels
cards.explanation: The end plate potential is graded: its size depends on how much acetylcholine was released and how many receptor channels opened, and it spreads passively to the surrounding sarcolemma. It is not all or none, because the end plate membrane itself is packed with ligand gated channels rather than voltage gated Na+ channels, which live in the folds just outside the end plate and generate the muscle action potential. Nothing at the end plate hyperpolarizes the fiber, and the response is far too fast to involve a second messenger cascade.

cards.q: When the nicotinic receptor channel opens, what net ion movement produces the end plate potential?
cards.a: Na+ entry exceeds K+ exit, so net positive charge moves in.
options: Cl- entry carries the current inward
K+ exit exceeds Na+ entry, so net positive charge moves out
Na+ entry exceeds K+ exit, so net positive charge moves in
Ca2+ entry alone carries the current
cards.explanation: The nicotinic receptor is a nonselective cation channel, so both Na+ and K+ move through it, but the driving force on Na+ at the resting potential is much larger than the driving force on K+. The result is a net inward positive current and a depolarization toward about 0 mV. If K+ exit dominated, the fiber would hyperpolarize and never fire. Ca2+ passes the channel only in trace amounts, and Cl- does not use this pathway at all.

cards.q: Where are the voltage gated Na+ channels that actually launch the muscle fiber action potential concentrated?
cards.a: In the junctional folds of the sarcolemma just outside the end plate.
options: In the presynaptic axon terminal membrane
In the junctional folds of the sarcolemma just outside the end plate
Spread evenly over the entire fiber surface at equal density
In the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane
cards.explanation: The end plate membrane is folded, and the depths of those folds hold a very high density of voltage gated Na+ channels sitting right next to the acetylcholine receptors on the crests. That arrangement means the local end plate depolarization reaches threshold at the shortest possible distance. The sarcoplasmic reticulum holds Ca2+ release channels, not the Na+ channels that fire the surface action potential. Terminal Na+ channels belong to the nerve, and although Na+ channels do continue along the whole fiber, their density is far higher at the junction.

cards.q: What does the term safety factor mean at the neuromuscular junction?
cards.a: The end plate potential far exceeds the depolarization needed to reach threshold.
options: Acetylcholinesterase removes transmitter fast enough to prevent damage to the receptor
The refractory period prevents the muscle fiber from firing twice to one nerve impulse
The muscle fiber can fire only after several nerve action potentials arrive together
The end plate potential far exceeds the depolarization needed to reach threshold
cards.explanation: A normal nerve impulse releases far more acetylcholine than the minimum needed, so the end plate potential overshoots threshold by a wide margin and transmission is reliably one for one. Skeletal muscle needs no summation of nerve impulses, which is what separates the neuromuscular junction from most central synapses. Cleft enzyme activity and the muscle refractory period are real features of the junction, but neither is what safety factor names.

cards.q: Curare competes with acetylcholine for the nicotinic receptor without opening the channel. What happens to the end plate potential?
cards.a: It shrinks, and if it falls below threshold the fiber does not fire.
options: It is unchanged, because the muscle action potential is generated independently
It grows larger because acetylcholine accumulates in the cleft
It shrinks, and if it falls below threshold the fiber does not fire
It becomes a hyperpolarization instead of a depolarization
cards.explanation: Fewer receptor channels open, so less inward cation current flows and the graded end plate potential is smaller. Enough curare drives it under threshold and the fiber stays silent, which is flaccid paralysis. Curare does not stop release, so acetylcholine does not build to a level that helps. It also does not open a chloride pathway, and the muscle action potential is not independent: it exists only because the end plate potential reaches threshold.

cards.q: Botulinum toxin cleaves the proteins that let synaptic vesicles fuse with the terminal membrane. Predict what happens at the junction.
cards.a: Acetylcholine is not released, so no end plate potential forms and the muscle is flaccid.
options: The receptors are blocked, so acetylcholine builds up in the cleft
The muscle fires normally but cannot release Ca2+ from its sarcoplasmic reticulum
Acetylcholine is released continuously, so the muscle stays contracted
Acetylcholine is not released, so no end plate potential forms and the muscle is flaccid
cards.explanation: Release is the step that fails, so the nerve action potential and the Ca2+ entry it causes are both normal but no transmitter crosses the cleft. With no end plate potential there is no muscle action potential and the fiber goes limp. Continuous release is the opposite problem and is what latrotoxin does. Botulinum leaves the receptors untouched, and it acts on the nerve rather than on excitation contraction coupling inside the fiber.

cards.q: A nerve muscle preparation is bathed in a solution containing no Ca2+. The motor nerve is stimulated and an action potential travels to the terminal. What happens next?
cards.a: No vesicles fuse, so no acetylcholine is released.
options: The nerve action potential fails before it reaches the terminal
Release continues normally because the vesicles are already docked
No vesicles fuse, so no acetylcholine is released
Release doubles because Ca2+ normally inhibits fusion
cards.explanation: Vesicle fusion is triggered by Ca2+ entering through voltage gated channels in the terminal, so with no extracellular Ca2+ there is no trigger and docked vesicles simply stay docked. Ca2+ promotes fusion rather than inhibiting it. The axonal action potential itself depends on Na+ and K+, not Ca2+, so it still arrives at the terminal, which is exactly why this experiment isolates the release step.

cards.q: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies reduce the number of functioning nicotinic receptors at the end plate. What is the immediate consequence?
cards.a: The end plate potential is smaller, so the safety factor falls.
options: The end plate potential is smaller, so the safety factor falls
The muscle fiber cannot release Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Acetylcholinesterase activity in the cleft rises sharply
Acetylcholine release from the nerve is reduced
cards.explanation: With fewer channels available to open, the same amount of acetylcholine produces less inward current and a smaller end plate potential, so the margin over threshold shrinks and some fibers fail to fire. Release from the nerve terminal is normal in myasthenia gravis, which is what distinguishes it from a presynaptic disorder. Ca2+ handling inside the fiber and the amount of cleft enzyme are not the primary lesion, although raising acetylcholine by inhibiting that enzyme is a rational way to compensate.

cards.q: A drug blocks acetylcholinesterase for a few minutes. What happens to acetylcholine in the cleft and to the end plate potential?
cards.a: Acetylcholine lingers, so the end plate potential is larger and lasts longer.
options: Acetylcholine is cleared faster, so the end plate potential is briefer
Acetylcholine lingers, so the end plate potential is larger and lasts longer
Acetylcholine is never released, so the end plate potential disappears
Acetylcholine binds a different receptor, so the end plate hyperpolarizes
cards.explanation: The enzyme is what normally clears transmitter in a couple of milliseconds, so blocking it leaves acetylcholine free to rebind receptors repeatedly and the end plate stays depolarized much longer than usual. That is useful in small doses, for example in myasthenia gravis, but a large dose holds the end plate depolarized so long that the fiber cannot fire again. Clearance cannot speed up when the clearing enzyme is gone, release is unaffected, and acetylcholine still acts on the same nicotinic receptor.

cards.q: A toxin blocks voltage gated Na+ channels in the sarcolemma but leaves nicotinic receptors intact. What do you record at the end plate?
cards.a: A normal end plate potential with no muscle action potential following it.
options: A hyperpolarization at the end plate instead of a depolarization
No end plate potential and no muscle action potential
A normal end plate potential with no muscle action potential following it
A normal muscle action potential with no end plate potential preceding it
cards.explanation: The end plate potential is produced by ligand gated cation channels, so it appears normally even when voltage gated Na+ channels are poisoned. What fails is the next step, the regenerative action potential in the surrounding sarcolemma, so the depolarization stays local and dies away. Blocking receptors instead would remove the end plate potential, and an action potential cannot appear without the end plate potential that triggers it.

cards.q: A motor neuron fires 20 action potentials in one second at a healthy junction. How many action potentials does the muscle fiber fire?
cards.a: Twenty, because transmission is one for one.
options: Twenty, because transmission is one for one
About forty, because each end plate potential triggers a burst
None, because 20 Hz is below the threshold frequency for the junction
About five, because several nerve impulses must summate
cards.explanation: The large safety factor means every nerve action potential produces an end plate potential well above threshold, so the muscle fiber fires once for each nerve impulse. Summation of successive nerve impulses is needed at typical central synapses, not here. Acetylcholinesterase clears the transmitter fast enough that one end plate potential does not set off a burst, and there is no minimum frequency for transmission.

cards.q: A patient with myasthenia gravis has the motor nerve stimulated repeatedly at 3 Hz. Normally the amount of acetylcholine released declines slightly over the first few stimuli. Predict the recorded muscle force.
cards.a: Force declines over successive stimuli, as more end plate potentials fall below threshold.
options: Force stays constant, because the safety factor covers the normal decline in release
Force increases over successive stimuli, because Ca2+ accumulates in the nerve terminal
Force stays constant, because the fibers themselves are normal and generate full twitches
Force declines over successive stimuli, as more end plate potentials fall below threshold
cards.explanation: Two facts combine here. Release normally dips a little during a low frequency train, and in myasthenia gravis the end plate potential already sits close to threshold, so that small dip pushes more fibers under threshold with each stimulus and recorded force falls. In a healthy junction the same decline in release is invisible because the safety factor absorbs it, which is exactly the answer that is true for a normal person and not for this patient. Terminal Ca2+ accumulation matters at much higher frequencies, and although the fibers are indeed normal, they never receive the signal to contract.

cards.q: An organophosphate insecticide irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase. After a brief period of twitching, the muscle becomes weak and unresponsive. What explains the weakness?
cards.a: Acetylcholine holds the end plate depolarized, so Na+ channels stay inactivated.
options: The sarcoplasmic reticulum runs out of Ca2+ to release to the thin filament
Acetylcholine holds the end plate depolarized, so Na+ channels stay inactivated
Acetylcholine is depleted from the terminal, so no more transmitter can be released
The nicotinic receptors are destroyed by the excess transmitter
cards.explanation: With no enzyme to clear it, acetylcholine keeps the receptor channels open and the end plate sits depolarized. Sustained depolarization drives the neighboring voltage gated Na+ channels into their inactivated state, and an inactivated channel cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes, so the fiber falls silent. This is a depolarizing block, and the striking point is that the muscle is paralyzed by too much transmitter rather than too little. Transmitter is not depleted here, the receptors survive, and sarcoplasmic reticulum stores are not the limiting factor at this stage.

cards.q: A toxin reduces the number of voltage gated Ca2+ channels in the motor nerve terminal. At rest, single stimuli produce weak contractions, but during a brief burst of rapid stimulation the contractions get stronger. Why?
cards.a: Ca2+ from successive impulses accumulates in the terminal, so more vesicles fuse per impulse.
options: Ca2+ from successive impulses accumulates in the terminal, so more vesicles fuse per impulse
The muscle fibers become more sensitive to acetylcholine within milliseconds
Voltage gated Na+ channels in the sarcolemma become easier to open at high frequency
Acetylcholinesterase is overwhelmed, so transmitter accumulates in the cleft
cards.explanation: Each impulse admits less Ca2+ than normal, so a single stimulus releases too few vesicles for a full end plate potential. During a fast train, Ca2+ from one impulse has not been pumped out before the next arrives, terminal Ca2+ builds up, and release per impulse climbs back toward normal. The lesion is presynaptic, so the cleft enzyme and the receptors on the muscle side are not what changes. Sarcolemmal Na+ channels do not become easier to open with rapid firing; if anything, repeated firing leaves more of them inactivated.

cards.q: A muscle is treated with a low dose of curare that leaves the end plate potential just barely above threshold. An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor is then added. Predict the effect on transmission and explain the mechanism.
cards.a: Transmission improves, because transmitter stays in the cleft longer and competes better for free receptors.
options: Transmission improves, because transmitter stays in the cleft longer and competes better for free receptors
Transmission is unchanged, because curare acts on the receptor and the inhibitor acts on the nerve terminal
Transmission improves, because the inhibitor increases the number of vesicles released per impulse
Transmission fails completely, because the two drugs both reduce receptor availability
cards.explanation: Curare and acetylcholine compete for the same binding sites, so the outcome depends on their relative concentrations at the receptor. Slowing the breakdown of acetylcholine raises its effective concentration and its dwell time, tipping the competition back toward transmitter and restoring a safe margin over threshold. The inhibitor works on the muscle side of the cleft, not on the nerve terminal, and it changes how long the released transmitter lasts rather than how much is released.

cards.q: What is a T tubule?
cards.a: An inward extension of the sarcolemma that carries the action potential inward.
options: A channel in the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane that releases Ca2+ to the cytosol
A protein bridge that links actin to the sarcolemma
An inward extension of the sarcolemma that carries the action potential inward
A closed internal sac that stores Ca2+ next to the myofibrils
cards.explanation: T tubules are continuous with the surface membrane and open to the extracellular fluid, so the action potential propagates down them and reaches every myofibril at nearly the same instant. The internal Ca2+ store is the sarcoplasmic reticulum, a separate closed compartment that is not continuous with the outside. The release channel and the structural linkages between filaments and membrane are proteins, not the tubule itself.

cards.q: Where is the dihydropyridine receptor located and what does it sense?
cards.a: In the T tubule membrane, where it senses voltage.
options: In the sarcolemma at the end plate, where it senses acetylcholine
In the thin filament, where it senses tropomyosin position
In the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane, where it senses Ca2+
In the T tubule membrane, where it senses voltage
cards.explanation: The dihydropyridine receptor is an L type Ca2+ channel sitting in the T tubule membrane, and in skeletal muscle its main job is to act as a voltage sensor that changes shape when the T tubule depolarizes. Placing it in the sarcoplasmic reticulum confuses it with the ryanodine receptor, which is the release channel it controls. It does not bind acetylcholine and it is a membrane protein, not part of the thin filament.

cards.q: What does the ryanodine receptor do?
cards.a: It is the Ca2+ release channel in the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane.
options: It pumps Ca2+ from the cytosol back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
It is the Ca2+ release channel in the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane
It binds Ca2+ inside the sarcoplasmic reticulum lumen
It is the voltage sensor in the T tubule membrane
cards.explanation: The ryanodine receptor is a large channel in the terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and when it opens Ca2+ pours out into the cytosol. Pumping Ca2+ back in is the job of SERCA, and buffering Ca2+ inside the lumen is the job of calsequestrin. The T tubule voltage sensor is the dihydropyridine receptor, which physically opens the ryanodine receptor.

cards.q: In skeletal muscle, how does the dihydropyridine receptor open the ryanodine receptor?
cards.a: By direct mechanical coupling, since the two proteins physically touch.
options: By admitting extracellular Ca2+ that then binds and opens the release channel
By direct mechanical coupling, since the two proteins physically touch
Through a second messenger released into the cytosol
By depolarizing the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane electrically
cards.explanation: In skeletal muscle the two proteins are physically linked across the narrow gap of the triad, so the conformational change in the voltage sensor tugs the release channel open with no chemical intermediate. Ca2+ induced Ca2+ release, where entering Ca2+ opens the channel, is the cardiac mechanism and is a favorite point of confusion between the two muscle types. There is no second messenger step and the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane is not depolarized by the action potential.

cards.q: What structures form a triad in skeletal muscle?
cards.a: One T tubule and the two terminal cisternae beside it.
options: One T tubule and the two terminal cisternae beside it
Three sarcomeres arranged end to end within a single myofibril
One sarcolemma with two mitochondria pressed against it
Three myofibrils bundled inside one sarcolemma
cards.explanation: The triad is the functional unit of excitation contraction coupling: the central T tubule carries the electrical signal and the two flanking cisternae hold the Ca2+ that will be released. This close apposition is what allows the voltage sensor and the release channel to touch. Counting myofibrils, sarcomeres, or mitochondria describes other features of muscle organization and none of them make the electrical to chemical link.

cards.q: Which protein inside the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds Ca2+ and keeps the free Ca2+ concentration in the lumen low?
cards.a: Calsequestrin.
options: Troponin C
Calmodulin
Calsequestrin
Titin
cards.explanation: Calsequestrin sits in the lumen and binds large amounts of Ca2+ loosely, which lets the sarcoplasmic reticulum store a big total load while keeping free luminal Ca2+ low enough that SERCA can keep pumping against it. Troponin C is the cytosolic Ca2+ sensor on the thin filament, and calmodulin is the Ca2+ binding protein that regulates smooth muscle rather than skeletal thin filaments. Titin is the elastic structural protein running from the Z disc to the thick filament.

cards.q: When ryanodine receptors open, which way does Ca2+ move and why?
cards.a: Out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol, down its concentration gradient.
options: Into the cell from the extracellular fluid, down its concentration gradient
Out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol, down its concentration gradient
Into the sarcoplasmic reticulum from the cytosol, down its concentration gradient
Out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol, pumped against its gradient
cards.explanation: Ca2+ is stored at a far higher concentration inside the sarcoplasmic reticulum than in the cytosol, so opening a channel lets it flow outward passively with no ATP required. Movement in the other direction is uphill and needs the SERCA pump. Release into the cytosol from outside the cell is the cardiac trigger step, not the main skeletal source, and a channel by definition cannot pump.

cards.q: Roughly how much does cytosolic free Ca2+ change between a resting and a fully activated skeletal muscle fiber?
cards.a: It rises about a hundredfold, from roughly 0.1 micromolar to roughly 10 micromolar.
options: It rises about a hundredfold, from roughly 1 millimolar to roughly 100 millimolar
It rises about twofold, from roughly 5 micromolar to roughly 10 micromolar
It rises about a hundredfold, from roughly 0.1 micromolar to roughly 10 micromolar
It falls about a hundredfold, from roughly 10 micromolar to roughly 0.1 micromolar
cards.explanation: Resting cytosolic free Ca2+ is held near 0.1 micromolar, which is far too low to occupy troponin, and release raises it into the micromolar range where troponin C sites fill. A large fold change is what makes Ca2+ a usable signal, so a mere doubling would not switch contraction on and off cleanly. A fall in Ca2+ is what happens during relaxation, and millimolar cytosolic Ca2+ would be toxic and would precipitate cellular phosphate.

cards.q: A skeletal muscle fiber is placed in a bath containing no Ca2+ at all. The nerve is bypassed and the fiber is stimulated directly. What happens?
cards.a: It still contracts, because the Ca2+ for contraction comes from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
options: It still contracts, because the Ca2+ for contraction comes from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
It contracts more strongly, because the Ca2+ gradient out of the cell is steeper
It contracts once and then cannot contract again for several minutes
It fails to contract, because Ca2+ must enter through the dihydropyridine receptor first
cards.explanation: Skeletal excitation contraction coupling is mechanical, so the voltage sensor opens the release channel without needing any Ca2+ to cross the surface membrane, and the internal store supplies everything the thin filament needs. A cardiac cell in the same bath would fail within a few beats, because it depends on Ca2+ induced Ca2+ release. Removing external Ca2+ does not strengthen contraction, and the internal store holds enough for many contractions.

cards.q: A high concentration of ryanodine locks the ryanodine receptor closed. The muscle action potential is recorded and is completely normal. What do you predict for contraction?
cards.a: No contraction, because Ca2+ never reaches the thin filament.
options: No contraction, because Ca2+ never reaches the thin filament
A sustained contracture, because Ca2+ cannot be pumped back
A weak contraction that builds slowly over several seconds
Normal contraction, because the action potential is normal
cards.explanation: The electrical signal and the mechanical response are separate steps, and this drug cuts the link between them: the T tubule depolarizes and the voltage sensor moves, but the release channel will not open, so cytosolic Ca2+ stays at resting level and tropomyosin never uncovers the binding sites. A normal action potential therefore guarantees nothing about force. A contracture requires Ca2+ to be high, which is the opposite of what happens here, and a slow weak contraction would still require some release.

cards.q: A treatment strips away the T tubules but leaves the surface membrane, the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and the contractile proteins intact. What is the effect of stimulating the fiber?
cards.a: The surface fires normally but the interior is not activated, so force is small.
options: Force is greater than normal, because the sarcoplasmic reticulum is no longer restrained
The surface fires normally but the interior is not activated, so force is small
No action potential occurs at all, because T tubules carry the surface current
Force is normal, because Ca2+ diffuses quickly enough from the surface to the center
cards.explanation: The T tubule system exists because a fiber is far too thick for a surface signal to activate the core in time, so removing it leaves only the outermost myofibrils responding and the whole fiber generates little force. The surface membrane still has its own Na+ channels, so the action potential itself is unaffected. Diffusion of a signal from the surface to the center of a fiber tens of micrometers across takes far longer than a twitch, which is precisely the problem T tubules solve.

cards.q: Malignant hyperthermia is caused by a ryanodine receptor that opens too easily and closes poorly. Predict the effect on cytosolic Ca2+ and on the muscle.
cards.a: Cytosolic Ca2+ stays high, producing sustained contracture and heat generation.
options: Cytosolic Ca2+ is normal, but the muscle cannot generate an action potential
Cytosolic Ca2+ stays low, producing flaccid paralysis
Cytosolic Ca2+ stays high, producing sustained contracture and heat generation
Cytosolic Ca2+ oscillates, producing a normal but faster twitch
cards.explanation: A leaky release channel keeps dumping Ca2+ into the cytosol faster than SERCA can retrieve it, so the thin filament stays switched on and the muscle stiffens. The heat comes from the enormous ATP consumption of both the crossbridges and the pump working against the leak. Low cytosolic Ca2+ would cause weakness rather than rigidity, and the defect is downstream of the action potential, which remains normal.

cards.q: Dantrolene reduces Ca2+ release through the ryanodine receptor. What effect does it have on a normal twitch?
cards.a: The twitch is weaker, because less Ca2+ reaches troponin.
options: The twitch is stronger, because Ca2+ stays in the store for the next stimulus
The twitch is unchanged, because the action potential is unchanged
The twitch is longer, because Ca2+ removal is slowed
The twitch is weaker, because less Ca2+ reaches troponin
cards.explanation: Force depends on how many troponin sites are occupied, so cutting the size of the Ca2+ transient means fewer exposed binding sites and less force. Saving Ca2+ in the store does not help the current twitch, since force is set by cytosolic Ca2+ at that moment. The action potential is upstream and untouched, and the drug acts on release rather than on the SERCA pump that governs how long the transient lasts.

cards.q: A mutation leaves the dihydropyridine receptor able to sense voltage and change shape but unable to conduct Ca2+ into the cell. What happens to skeletal muscle contraction?
cards.a: It is essentially normal, because the sensor function opens the channel.
options: It is essentially normal, because the sensor function opens the channel
It becomes slower but eventually reaches nearly normal force
It becomes stronger, because Ca2+ no longer competes at the thin filament
It fails completely, because entering Ca2+ is what triggers release
cards.explanation: In skeletal muscle the dihydropyridine receptor works as a mechanical switch, and the small Ca2+ current it carries is not needed for coupling. That is why the same mutation would be devastating in cardiac muscle, where the entering Ca2+ is the trigger for Ca2+ induced Ca2+ release. Contraction does not become slow or strong here, because the pathway that matters is unchanged.

cards.q: Put these events in the correct order: Ca2+ binds troponin, T tubule depolarizes, ryanodine receptor opens, dihydropyridine receptor changes shape.
cards.a: T tubule depolarizes, dihydropyridine receptor changes shape, ryanodine receptor opens, Ca2+ binds troponin.
options: T tubule depolarizes, dihydropyridine receptor changes shape, ryanodine receptor opens, Ca2+ binds troponin
Dihydropyridine receptor changes shape, T tubule depolarizes, Ca2+ binds troponin, ryanodine receptor opens
Ryanodine receptor opens, T tubule depolarizes, dihydropyridine receptor changes shape, Ca2+ binds troponin
T tubule depolarizes, ryanodine receptor opens, dihydropyridine receptor changes shape, Ca2+ binds troponin
cards.explanation: The signal runs from electrical to mechanical to chemical: depolarization moves down the T tubule, the voltage sensor in that membrane changes conformation, the change pulls the release channel open, and only then does Ca2+ reach the thin filament. Any order that opens the release channel before the sensor moves reverses the direction of the mechanical link. The T tubule must depolarize first, because it is the arrival of the action potential that starts the whole sequence.

cards.q: A fiber has a normal action potential, a sarcoplasmic reticulum loaded with Ca2+, and normal contractile proteins, yet direct stimulation produces almost no force. Adding caffeine, which opens ryanodine receptors directly, produces a strong contracture. Where is the lesion?
cards.a: In the link from the voltage sensor to the release channel.
options: In the sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ store
In the link from the voltage sensor to the release channel
In the crossbridge cycle inside the myofibrils
In the acetylcholine receptors of the motor end plate
cards.explanation: Caffeine bypasses the voltage sensor and opens the release channel chemically, so a strong response to caffeine proves that the store is full, the release channel works, and the contractile machinery can generate force. The only step left untested by caffeine is the mechanical link from the T tubule sensor to the channel, and that is exactly the step that stimulation depends on. The end plate is irrelevant because the fiber was stimulated directly.

cards.q: Two preparations, a skeletal fiber and a cardiac cell, are both switched to a Ca2+ free bath and stimulated repeatedly. Predict what happens to each.
cards.a: The skeletal fiber keeps contracting while the cardiac cell soon stops.
options: Both stop, because both need entering Ca2+ as a trigger
The cardiac cell keeps contracting while the skeletal fiber soon stops
Both keep contracting, because both use internal stores
The skeletal fiber keeps contracting while the cardiac cell soon stops
cards.explanation: Both cell types release Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, but they differ in what opens the release channel. Skeletal coupling is mechanical and needs no external Ca2+, while cardiac coupling depends on Ca2+ entering through L type channels to trigger Ca2+ induced Ca2+ release, and cardiac stores also run down without that influx. This single experiment is the classic way to demonstrate the difference between the two coupling mechanisms.

cards.q: A patient with a leaky ryanodine receptor is given a drug that causes prolonged end plate depolarization and repeated muscle action potentials. Body temperature climbs and the muscles stiffen. Trace why the temperature rises.
cards.a: Ca2+ stays high, so crossbridges cycle and SERCA pumps constantly, and both consume ATP that appears as heat.
options: The repeated action potentials themselves consume most of the ATP, and the pumping of Na+ and K+ releases the heat
The stiff muscle compresses blood vessels, so the body cannot carry heat away from the limbs
The leaky channel releases stored chemical energy directly as heat when it opens
Ca2+ stays high, so crossbridges cycle and SERCA pumps constantly, and both consume ATP that appears as heat
cards.explanation: Heat production tracks ATP turnover, and here two large consumers are running at once: myosin heads cycling against a thin filament that never switches off, and SERCA pumping hard against a channel that keeps leaking Ca2+ back out. Restoring Na+ and K+ after action potentials does cost ATP, but that cost is small next to the contractile and pumping load. Reduced heat loss is not the driver, and an open channel releases no meaningful heat on its own since Ca2+ is moving down its gradient.

cards.q: In a fatigued fiber, the action potential is normal and troponin still responds to Ca2+ normally, but the measured Ca2+ transient is smaller than in a rested fiber. Which step of excitation contraction coupling best accounts for the reduced force?
cards.a: Reduced Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum per impulse.
options: Reduced acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
Reduced sensitivity of the thin filament to Ca2+
Reduced Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum per impulse
Failure of the action potential to propagate into the T tubules
cards.explanation: The measurements pin the lesion for you. A normal action potential rules out both the junction and propagation, and a normal troponin response rules out a change in thin filament sensitivity, so the only remaining explanation for a smaller Ca2+ transient is that less Ca2+ leaves the store per impulse. Reduced release, from partly depleted stores and inhibited release channels, is in fact a major contributor to fatigue in real muscle.

cards.q: Which part of which protein carries the ATPase activity that powers contraction?
cards.a: The head of the myosin molecule.
options: The troponin complex on the thin filament
The actin monomer itself
The head of the myosin molecule
The tail of the myosin molecule
cards.explanation: The globular myosin head contains both the actin binding site and the site that binds and hydrolyzes ATP, which is why the same structure that grabs the thin filament is also the motor. The myosin tail packs into the backbone of the thick filament and does no chemistry. Troponin is the Ca2+ switch on the thin filament and actin provides the track, but neither hydrolyzes the ATP that drives cycling.

cards.q: What causes the myosin head to let go of actin at the end of a crossbridge cycle?
cards.a: A fresh ATP molecule binds to the myosin head.
options: A fresh ATP molecule binds to the myosin head
Ca2+ leaves troponin C
Phosphate is released from the myosin head
ATP is hydrolyzed on the myosin head
cards.explanation: Binding, not hydrolysis, is what breaks the bond: when ATP occupies the nucleotide site the affinity of the head for actin drops sharply and the crossbridge detaches. Hydrolysis comes immediately afterward and re cocks the detached head. Ca2+ leaving troponin ends the whole contraction rather than a single cycle, and phosphate release is the trigger for the power stroke earlier in the cycle.

cards.q: What does hydrolysis of ATP on the detached myosin head accomplish?
cards.a: It cocks the head into its high energy position.
options: It drives the power stroke that pulls the thin filament
It cocks the head into its high energy position
It releases the head from actin
It opens the myosin binding site on actin
cards.explanation: Splitting ATP into ADP and inorganic phosphate transfers energy into the myosin head and rotates it into the cocked, high energy conformation, with both products still bound. The power stroke happens later, when the head is attached and phosphate leaves. Detachment is caused by ATP binding rather than by its hydrolysis, and uncovering the binding site on actin is the job of Ca2+ and tropomyosin.

cards.q: Release of which molecule from the attached myosin head triggers the power stroke?
cards.a: Phosphate.
options: ADP
Phosphate
ATP
Ca2+
cards.explanation: Once the cocked head binds actin, the loss of inorganic phosphate lets it swivel and drag the thin filament toward the center of the sarcomere. ADP leaves at the end of the stroke, after the movement has occurred, and the empty site is then available for a new ATP. ATP is not released from the head, it is consumed, and Ca2+ is released from troponin at the end of a contraction rather than at each stroke.

cards.q: What is the rigor state of a crossbridge?
cards.a: Myosin bound tightly to actin with an empty nucleotide site.
options: Myosin bound loosely to actin with ATP in its binding site
Myosin bound tightly to actin with an empty nucleotide site
Myosin detached from actin with ATP in its binding site
Myosin cocked and detached with ADP and phosphate bound
cards.explanation: After the power stroke and ADP release, the head sits firmly attached with an empty nucleotide site, and it stays that way until a new ATP arrives. That is the rigor complex, and its persistence when ATP runs out is what stiffens muscle after death. The cocked detached state and the ATP bound detached state are both normal steps of the cycle that require nucleotide to be present.

cards.q: During the power stroke, what moves?
cards.a: The thin filament slides toward the center of the sarcomere.
options: The thick filament shortens as its myosin molecules contract
The thin filament slides toward the center of the sarcomere
Both filaments shorten by about the same fraction
The Z discs thicken while the filaments stay in place
cards.explanation: Contraction is sliding, not shortening of filaments: the myosin head swivels and pulls actin inward, so the sarcomere narrows while both sets of filaments keep their original length. That is the central claim of the sliding filament model, and it is what the banding pattern under a microscope confirms. Filaments do not contract on their own, and the Z disc is drawn inward rather than thickened.

cards.q: Which sequence correctly orders one crossbridge cycle, starting from a cocked head and an exposed binding site?
cards.a: Binding, power stroke, detachment, reactivation.
options: Binding, power stroke, detachment, reactivation
Reactivation, detachment, binding, power stroke
Binding, detachment, power stroke, reactivation
Power stroke, binding, reactivation, detachment
cards.explanation: A cocked head attaches to actin, swivels to pull the filament, is released when new ATP binds, and is then re cocked by hydrolysis so the cycle can repeat. Detaching before the power stroke would mean the head never pulls anything. Reactivation cannot come before detachment either, since the head has to be free before hydrolysis can reset it.

cards.q: How many ATP molecules are consumed by one myosin head in one complete crossbridge cycle?
cards.a: One.
options: Four
None, because the energy comes from the Ca2+ gradient
One
Two
cards.explanation: Each cycle uses a single ATP: it binds to release the head, and its hydrolysis re cocks that head for the next attachment. Force is scaled up by having many heads cycling many times, not by spending more ATP per stroke. The Ca2+ gradient controls whether cycling can occur but supplies none of the mechanical energy, which comes entirely from ATP.

cards.q: After death, ATP production stops and muscles become stiff. Why does rigor mortis develop?
cards.a: Without ATP to bind, myosin heads cannot detach from actin.
options: Without ATP, myosin heads cannot be cocked, so they freeze mid stroke
Without ATP, tropomyosin permanently covers the binding sites
Without ATP, Ca2+ cannot be released, so the filaments lock in place
Without ATP to bind, myosin heads cannot detach from actin
cards.explanation: Detachment is the only step of the cycle that requires ATP simply to bind, so when the supply runs out the heads that are attached stay attached and the muscle becomes rigid. Ca2+ also leaks into the cytosol because SERCA has no ATP, which keeps the binding sites exposed and lets more heads attach. A head that cannot be cocked is a detached head, which would leave muscle limp rather than stiff, and covered binding sites would also mean no attachment at all.

cards.q: A muscle fiber has plenty of ATP but its cytosolic Ca2+ stays at resting level. What is the state of the crossbridges?
cards.a: Detached and cocked, unable to bind because the sites are covered.
options: Attached but unable to complete the power stroke
Attached and locked, because there is nothing to release them
Detached and cocked, unable to bind because the sites are covered
Cycling slowly, because a few sites are always exposed
cards.explanation: With ATP available the heads are hydrolyzing it and sitting in the cocked, high energy state, but tropomyosin still covers the myosin binding sites on actin, so there is nowhere to attach and the muscle is relaxed. This is the normal resting condition of muscle. Locked attachment describes rigor, which requires the absence of ATP, and a stalled power stroke would require the head to be bound in the first place.

cards.q: A drug prevents inorganic phosphate from leaving the attached myosin head. What happens to force production?
cards.a: Force falls, because heads attach but cannot complete the power stroke.
options: Force rises, because heads stay attached longer
Force falls, because heads attach but cannot complete the power stroke
Force is unchanged, because phosphate release is not part of the cycle
Force rises briefly and then the muscle enters rigor
cards.explanation: Phosphate release is the step that lets the cocked head swivel, so blocking it strands heads in a weakly bound state that generates little tension. Staying attached is only useful if the attachment is a force generating one. Phosphate release is very much part of the cycle, and rigor is a different problem caused by lack of ATP rather than by a stalled phosphate step.

cards.q: A muscle fiber in rigor is bathed in a solution containing ATP but no Ca2+. What happens?
cards.a: The heads detach and the fiber relaxes.
options: The heads detach and the fiber relaxes
The fiber contracts strongly, because ATP is the energy source
The fiber stays rigid, because Ca2+ is needed for detachment
The heads detach and immediately reattach, producing sustained cycling
cards.explanation: ATP binding alone is enough to break the actin myosin bond, which is why adding ATP releases rigor even when Ca2+ is absent. Without Ca2+ the heads cannot reattach, so the fiber goes limp instead of contracting or cycling. Detachment requires ATP rather than Ca2+, and this experiment separates the two roles cleanly.

cards.q: Which change would allow a muscle to hold a given force while using less ATP?
cards.a: Myosin heads that stay attached longer during each cycle.
options: Myosin heads that stay attached longer during each cycle
A larger Ca2+ transient with each action potential
A faster SERCA pump in the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Myosin heads that hydrolyze ATP faster
cards.explanation: Force depends on how many heads are attached at any instant, so a head that spends a longer fraction of its cycle attached contributes the same tension for fewer ATP molecules per second. Slow postural muscle uses exactly this strategy. Faster hydrolysis speeds cycling and raises the ATP cost, a bigger Ca2+ transient does not change the cost of each cycle, and a faster pump increases ATP use rather than reducing it.

cards.q: During a maximal contraction, individual crossbridges are attaching and detaching continuously. Why does force look steady rather than jerky?
cards.a: Heads cycle out of step, so the attached fraction stays nearly constant.
options: Heads cycle out of step, so the attached fraction stays nearly constant
All heads attach and detach in synchrony many times per second
Force is smoothed by the elasticity of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Each head stays attached for the whole of the contraction
cards.explanation: With millions of heads cycling asynchronously, the number attached at any instant fluctuates only slightly, so tension is smooth even though every individual bridge is intermittent. If all heads worked in synchrony, force would in fact oscillate visibly. A head that never detached could not pull the filament any farther, and the sarcoplasmic reticulum is a Ca2+ store rather than a mechanical damper.

cards.q: Two fibers are identical except that fiber A has a myosin isoform that hydrolyzes ATP twice as fast. Predict fiber A's shortening velocity and ATP consumption compared with fiber B.
cards.a: Faster shortening and higher ATP consumption.
options: Slower shortening and higher ATP consumption
Faster shortening with no change in ATP consumption
Faster shortening and lower ATP consumption
Faster shortening and higher ATP consumption
cards.explanation: Maximum shortening velocity is set by how quickly myosin can complete cycles, so a faster ATPase means faster cycling and faster shortening. Each cycle still costs one ATP, so cycling faster necessarily costs more ATP per second, which is why fast fibers fatigue sooner. There is no way to speed cycling and spend less energy, and a fast ATPase cannot produce slow shortening.

cards.q: An inhibitor traps myosin in a detached state with ADP and phosphate still bound. Predict the fiber's stiffness and its rate of ATP use.
cards.a: Low stiffness and low ATP use, because heads neither attach nor complete cycles.
options: High stiffness and high ATP use, because heads cycle rapidly without producing force
High stiffness and low ATP use, because heads are locked onto actin
Low stiffness and low ATP use, because heads neither attach nor complete cycles
Low stiffness and high ATP use, because hydrolysis continues at full speed
cards.explanation: Stiffness in a muscle fiber reflects how many heads are physically attached, and here they are all detached, so the fiber is compliant and generates no force. ATP use also falls, because a head cannot bind and hydrolyze another ATP until it has completed the attachment and release steps of the cycle, so the cycle stalls rather than spinning. High stiffness would require attachment, which is exactly what this inhibitor prevents.

cards.q: A skinned muscle fiber is placed in a solution with high Ca2+ and no ATP. It is then switched to a solution with normal ATP and high Ca2+. Describe the two states.
cards.a: Rigid in the first solution, then actively contracting in the second.
options: Actively contracting in the first solution, then rigid in the second
Relaxed in the first solution, then actively contracting in the second
Rigid in the first solution, then relaxed in the second
Rigid in the first solution, then actively contracting in the second
cards.explanation: High Ca2+ exposes the binding sites, so heads attach, but with no ATP they cannot detach and the fiber locks in rigor. Adding ATP allows detachment, and because Ca2+ is still high the freed heads are re cocked and reattach, so the fiber cycles and generates active force. The fiber would only relax in the second solution if Ca2+ were also removed, which is the comparison worth keeping straight.

cards.q: Ischemia lowers ATP in a working muscle. Which step of the crossbridge cycle fails first, and what does the fiber feel like?
cards.a: Detachment fails first, so the fiber becomes stiff and difficult to move.
options: Attachment fails first, so the fiber becomes limp and easy to stretch
The power stroke fails first, so the fiber holds a fixed length with no stiffness
Reactivation fails first, so the fiber relaxes completely
Detachment fails first, so the fiber becomes stiff and difficult to move
cards.explanation: ATP is required at two points, to detach an attached head and to re cock the free head, and the detachment step is the one whose failure has an immediate mechanical consequence. Heads that cannot let go stay bound, so resistance to stretch rises and the muscle feels stiff, a state related to the cramping and rigidity of severe energy depletion. A limp fiber would require the heads to be detached, which is the opposite of what happens when ATP runs out.

cards.q: A fiber is stimulated and generates force, but a measurement shows that ATP consumption is far higher than expected for the force produced. Which change in the crossbridge cycle best explains it?
cards.a: Heads detach sooner after the power stroke, so fewer are attached at any moment.
options: Fewer myosin binding sites are exposed, so fewer heads can attach at all
ATP hydrolysis is blocked, so heads remain in the cocked state
Heads detach sooner after the power stroke, so fewer are attached at any moment
Heads stay attached longer, so more heads are attached at any moment
cards.explanation: ATP cost is set by how many cycles are completed per second while force is set by how many heads are attached at once, so anything that shortens the attached portion of the cycle raises the cost per unit of force. Longer attachment does the reverse and makes the muscle more economical. Fewer exposed sites would lower both force and ATP use together, and blocked hydrolysis would lower ATP use to nearly zero.

cards.q: Which subunit of the troponin complex binds Ca2+?
cards.a: Troponin C.
options: Troponin M
Troponin T
Troponin I
Troponin C
cards.explanation: Troponin C is the Ca2+ sensor of the thin filament, and the C in its name is a useful reminder. Troponin T is the subunit that binds tropomyosin, and troponin I is the subunit that holds the complex against actin and inhibits binding when Ca2+ is low. There is no troponin M in skeletal muscle, although calmodulin plays the Ca2+ sensing role in smooth muscle.

cards.q: What covers the myosin binding sites on actin in a resting skeletal muscle fiber?
cards.a: Tropomyosin.
options: Tropomyosin
Troponin C
Titin
Calsequestrin
cards.explanation: Tropomyosin is a long fibrous protein that lies in the groove of the actin helix and physically blocks the sites where myosin heads would attach. Troponin C does not block anything, it senses Ca2+ and repositions tropomyosin through the rest of the complex. Titin is the elastic protein running from the Z disc to the thick filament, and calsequestrin buffers Ca2+ inside the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

cards.q: Which three proteins make up the thin filament of skeletal muscle?
cards.a: Actin, tropomyosin, and troponin.
options: Actin, tropomyosin, and troponin
Myosin, tropomyosin, and calsequestrin
Actin, troponin, and calmodulin
Actin, myosin, and titin
cards.explanation: The thin filament is a double helix of actin monomers with tropomyosin lying along it and one troponin complex attached every seven actin monomers, and that arrangement is what makes the whole filament a Ca2+ controlled switch. Myosin belongs to the thick filament, and titin links the thick filament to the Z disc rather than forming part of the thin filament. Calsequestrin is inside the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and calmodulin is the Ca2+ sensor of smooth muscle.

cards.q: When cytosolic Ca2+ rises in skeletal muscle, which protein does it bind to start contraction?
cards.a: Troponin C on the thin filament.
options: Myosin light chain kinase in the cytosol
Calmodulin in the cytosol
Troponin C on the thin filament
The myosin head on the thick filament
cards.explanation: Skeletal muscle uses thin filament regulation: Ca2+ binds troponin C and the whole tropomyosin troponin assembly shifts to uncover the binding sites. Calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase form the Ca2+ pathway in smooth muscle, where regulation happens on the thick filament instead, and mixing the two systems is one of the most common errors in this unit. The myosin head binds ATP and actin, not Ca2+.

cards.q: What does troponin I do when cytosolic Ca2+ is low?
cards.a: It holds the complex against actin and inhibits binding.
options: It links the complex to tropomyosin
It pumps Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
It binds Ca2+ and changes the shape of the whole complex
It holds the complex against actin and inhibits binding
cards.explanation: Troponin I is the inhibitory subunit, and its grip on actin is what keeps tropomyosin parked over the myosin binding sites. When Ca2+ binds troponin C, troponin I loosens its hold and the whole assembly rolls aside. Binding Ca2+ is the job of troponin C, linking to tropomyosin is the job of troponin T, and Ca2+ pumping is done by SERCA.

cards.q: After Ca2+ binds troponin C, what happens to tropomyosin?
cards.a: It rolls deeper into the groove and uncovers the binding sites.
options: It slides along the thin filament toward the Z disc
It binds the myosin head directly and holds it away from actin
It detaches from the thin filament and diffuses away
It rolls deeper into the groove and uncovers the binding sites
cards.explanation: Tropomyosin stays attached but shifts its position within the groove, and that small movement is enough to expose the surface of actin that myosin needs. It does not leave the filament, since it must be able to slide back and block the sites again when Ca2+ falls. It does not travel lengthwise along the filament, and it blocks myosin by covering actin rather than by gripping the myosin head.

cards.q: Skeletal muscle regulation is described as thin filament regulation. What does that mean?
cards.a: The switch that permits crossbridge formation sits on actin rather than on myosin.
options: Ca2+ is stored in the thin filament until an action potential arrives
The thin filament shortens while the thick filament stays the same length
The switch that permits crossbridge formation sits on actin rather than on myosin
Only the thin filament requires ATP to work
cards.explanation: Calling it thin filament regulation means the control proteins, troponin and tropomyosin, ride on actin and decide whether myosin may attach, while the myosin heads themselves are always ready to cycle. Smooth muscle is regulated on the thick filament by phosphorylation of myosin instead. Neither filament shortens, ATP is used by myosin on the thick filament, and Ca2+ is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

cards.q: Roughly what cytosolic Ca2+ concentration is needed to begin activating the thin filament?
cards.a: About 1 micromolar.
options: About 1 nanomolar
About 1 micromolar
About 1 millimolar
About 1 mole per liter
cards.explanation: Troponin C sites begin to fill as cytosolic Ca2+ moves out of the resting range near 0.1 micromolar and approaches 1 micromolar, with force close to maximal around 10 micromolar. A nanomolar concentration is below resting level and would leave the filament fully switched off. Millimolar cytosolic Ca2+ never occurs in a living cell, and a molar concentration is far outside any physiological range.

cards.q: A fiber has a normal action potential, normal ATP, and normal contractile proteins, but its sarcoplasmic reticulum cannot release Ca2+. What happens when it is stimulated?
cards.a: No contraction, because tropomyosin stays over the binding sites.
options: A normal contraction that relaxes unusually slowly
A weak contraction, because some myosin heads bind anyway
No contraction, because tropomyosin stays over the binding sites
A sustained contracture, because the heads cannot detach
cards.explanation: Without a rise in cytosolic Ca2+, troponin C stays empty, troponin I keeps its grip on actin, and tropomyosin never moves, so no myosin head can attach no matter how much ATP is available. Blocking is essentially complete at resting Ca2+, so there is no residual weak contraction to speak of. A contracture requires attached heads and therefore high Ca2+, and slow relaxation would require a contraction to have happened first.

cards.q: A mutation leaves troponin C unable to bind Ca2+, although Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum is normal. Predict the Ca2+ measurement and the force.
cards.a: A normal Ca2+ transient with no force.
options: A normal Ca2+ transient with no force
No Ca2+ transient with normal force
A larger than normal Ca2+ transient with normal force
No Ca2+ transient and no force
cards.explanation: Release and detection are separate steps, so a fiber that releases Ca2+ but cannot detect it shows a perfectly ordinary Ca2+ signal while generating no tension at all. That dissociation is what identifies the lesion as being at the thin filament rather than in the release machinery, where the transient itself would be missing. Force can never be normal when the switch that permits crossbridge attachment is broken.

cards.q: A treatment removes troponin and tropomyosin from the thin filament while leaving actin, myosin, and ATP intact. What do you predict?
cards.a: Continuous crossbridge cycling at any Ca2+ concentration.
options: Cycling only when Ca2+ is high, exactly as before
Cycling only when Ca2+ is below the resting level
No crossbridge cycling at any Ca2+ concentration
Continuous crossbridge cycling at any Ca2+ concentration
cards.explanation: Troponin and tropomyosin exist to keep myosin off actin, so stripping them leaves the binding sites permanently exposed and the heads cycle as long as ATP lasts. This is the strongest evidence that Ca2+ does not activate myosin directly, it merely removes an inhibition. Cycling cannot become Ca2+ dependent when the Ca2+ sensing protein is gone, and it certainly does not reverse to require low Ca2+.

cards.q: A fiber is held at a cytosolic Ca2+ level partway between resting and maximal. What do you predict about force?
cards.a: Intermediate force, because only some troponin sites are occupied.
options: Intermediate force, because only some troponin sites are occupied
No force, because a threshold Ca2+ level must be exceeded for any activation
Intermediate force, because each crossbridge produces a smaller power stroke
Maximal force, because thin filament activation is all or none
cards.explanation: Activation is graded at the level of the filament: more Ca2+ means more occupied troponin complexes, more exposed actin, and more heads attached, which is why force rises smoothly with cytosolic Ca2+ over the micromolar range. Individual crossbridges do not produce partial strokes, so the grading comes from the number of active bridges rather than the size of each. All or none behavior belongs to the action potential, not to the thin filament.

cards.q: A fiber is bathed in high Ca2+ with plenty of ATP available. Compare it with an identical fiber in high Ca2+ with no ATP.
cards.a: The first cycles and produces force, the second locks in rigor.
options: Both relax, because Ca2+ alone cannot start contraction
Both lock in rigor, because high Ca2+ prevents detachment
The first cycles and produces force, the second locks in rigor
The first relaxes, the second cycles and produces force
cards.explanation: Ca2+ decides whether myosin may attach and ATP decides whether it can detach and re cock, so the two conditions separate the two controls neatly. With both present the fiber cycles normally, and with Ca2+ but no ATP the heads attach and stay attached in the rigor state. Ca2+ does not prevent detachment, ATP binding is what causes it.

cards.q: Caffeine at high concentration makes ryanodine receptors leak Ca2+ at rest. What effect on the thin filament and the muscle?
cards.a: Some binding sites stay uncovered, so the muscle develops a resting contracture.
options: Tropomyosin stays over the sites, so the muscle becomes flaccid
Some binding sites stay uncovered, so the muscle develops a resting contracture
Troponin C is destroyed, so the muscle cannot respond to further stimulation
Ca2+ binds myosin directly, so the heads cycle without actin
cards.explanation: Anything that keeps cytosolic Ca2+ above the activation threshold keeps troponin occupied and tropomyosin displaced, so crossbridges keep forming without an action potential and the muscle stiffens. Flaccidity would require the opposite, a fall in cytosolic Ca2+. Caffeine does not damage troponin, and Ca2+ never binds the myosin head in skeletal muscle, which is the thin filament versus thick filament distinction worth holding onto.

cards.q: Why does a drug that blocks Ca2+ release stop contraction even though ATP levels and myosin ATPase activity are normal?
cards.a: Myosin cannot attach to actin, and the ATPase stalls without actin.
options: Myosin cannot attach to actin, and the ATPase stalls without actin
Ca2+ rather than ATP is the direct source of energy for the stroke
The thick filament collapses without Ca2+ to support it
ATP cannot be hydrolyzed at all unless Ca2+ is present
cards.explanation: Ca2+ is a permission signal, not an energy source. Blocking its release leaves the heads cocked and full of ADP and phosphate with nowhere to attach, and because attachment and phosphate release are what drive the cycle forward, the ATPase effectively stalls. The energy for the stroke comes from ATP hydrolysis, and the thick filament is structurally stable regardless of Ca2+.

cards.q: Two fibers both fail to contract when stimulated. Fiber A shows no rise in cytosolic Ca2+, fiber B shows a normal rise. Where is the defect in each?
cards.a: Fiber A upstream of release, fiber B at the thin filament regulatory proteins.
options: Fiber A at the thin filament, fiber B upstream of release
Fiber A upstream of release, fiber B at the thin filament regulatory proteins
Both at the thin filament, since neither contracts
Both upstream of release, since Ca2+ measurement is unreliable during contraction
cards.explanation: The Ca2+ measurement splits the pathway in two. A missing transient means the failure lies at or before Ca2+ release, in the T tubule, the voltage sensor, or the release channel. A normal transient with no force means the signal arrived and was not acted on, which points to troponin, tropomyosin, or the crossbridge machinery itself. Reversing the two assignments ignores which half of the pathway the measurement actually tests.

cards.q: A fiber is exposed to a toxin that locks tropomyosin in its blocking position. Predict the action potential, the Ca2+ transient, and the force.
cards.a: Normal action potential, normal Ca2+ transient, no force.
options: Normal action potential, absent Ca2+ transient, no force
Normal action potential, normal Ca2+ transient, no force
Absent action potential, absent Ca2+ transient, no force
Normal action potential, normal Ca2+ transient, sustained contracture
cards.explanation: The toxin acts at the last regulatory step, so everything upstream proceeds normally: the fiber fires, the T tubule signal reaches the release channels, and Ca2+ floods the cytosol. What fails is the response to that Ca2+, because tropomyosin cannot move and the binding sites stay covered. A locked blocking position produces paralysis, not contracture, which is what a tropomyosin locked in the open position would cause.

cards.q: Force is measured in a skinned fiber while cytosolic Ca2+ is raised in steps from 0.05 micromolar to 20 micromolar. Describe the shape of the force curve and explain both ends.
cards.a: Force stays near zero at the lowest Ca2+, rises steeply, then plateaus once troponin is occupied.
options: Force rises in a straight line across the entire range, because each Ca2+ ion exposes one binding site
Force stays near zero at the lowest Ca2+, rises steeply, then plateaus once troponin is occupied
Force is maximal at the lowest Ca2+ and falls as Ca2+ rises and saturates troponin
Force rises steeply and then falls at high Ca2+, because excess Ca2+ blocks the myosin heads
cards.explanation: The curve has a flat foot, a steep middle, and a plateau. At resting Ca2+ almost no troponin sites are filled, so tropomyosin blocks nearly everything. Through the micromolar range each increment fills more sites and exposes more actin, and once the sites are saturated no further Ca2+ can uncover anything new, so force levels off. A straight line ignores both the resting block and the saturation, and high Ca2+ does not inhibit the heads.

cards.q: A fiber that has been stimulated repeatedly shows a normal sized Ca2+ transient but less force than when it was rested. What change at the thin filament could explain this?
cards.a: Reduced sensitivity of troponin C to the Ca2+ that arrives.
options: Loss of tropomyosin from the thin filament
Reduced Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Reduced sensitivity of troponin C to the Ca2+ that arrives
Failure of the action potential to invade the T tubules
cards.explanation: A normal transient rules out every step up to and including release, so the explanation has to lie in how the filament responds to Ca2+ rather than in how much Ca2+ arrives. Accumulating metabolites during repeated activity lower the affinity of troponin C for Ca2+, so an unchanged signal produces fewer occupied sites and less force. Reduced release and failed T tubule conduction would both shrink the measured transient, and losing tropomyosin would raise force rather than lower it.

cards.q: What does SERCA do?
cards.a: It pumps Ca2+ from the cytosol into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
options: It releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol
It pumps Ca2+ out of the cell across the sarcolemma
It binds Ca2+ inside the sarcoplasmic reticulum lumen
It pumps Ca2+ from the cytosol into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
cards.explanation: SERCA is a primary active transporter in the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane, and by clearing Ca2+ from the cytosol it both ends the current contraction and reloads the store for the next one. Release in the other direction is the job of the ryanodine receptor, which is a channel and uses no ATP. The plasma membrane Ca2+ pump handles export from the cell, and calsequestrin does the luminal buffering.

cards.q: What is the energy source for moving Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum?
cards.a: ATP hydrolyzed by the pump itself.
options: The membrane potential of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
The Na+ gradient across the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane
ATP hydrolyzed by the pump itself
The Ca2+ concentration gradient
cards.explanation: Ca2+ is being moved from about 1 micromolar in the cytosol into a store where its concentration is far higher, so the transport is uphill and must be paid for directly with ATP, which makes SERCA a primary active transporter. Its own concentration gradient points the wrong way and would drive Ca2+ back out. There is no Na+ gradient across this internal membrane to exploit, and the sarcoplasmic reticulum does not maintain a membrane potential that could power the pump.

cards.q: Where is acetylcholinesterase located and what does it accomplish?
cards.a: In the synaptic cleft, where it clears acetylcholine from the receptors.
options: In the sarcoplasmic reticulum, where it ends the Ca2+ transient
On the muscle membrane, where it opens the receptor channel
In the axon terminal, where it recycles acetylcholine into vesicles
In the synaptic cleft, where it clears acetylcholine from the receptors
cards.explanation: The enzyme is anchored in the basal lamina of the cleft, positioned to intercept acetylcholine within a millisecond or two of its release, and that speed is what allows the end plate potential to end so each nerve impulse produces exactly one muscle impulse. Vesicle loading happens in the terminal but uses a different transporter, the Ca2+ transient is ended by SERCA, and the enzyme destroys transmitter rather than opening channels.

cards.q: What are the products when acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine?
cards.a: Choline and acetate.
options: Choline and phosphate
Choline and acetate
Acetyl CoA and choline
Acetate and acetyl CoA
cards.explanation: The enzyme splits the ester bond to give choline and acetate, and the choline is then taken back up into the nerve terminal by a transporter and reused to make new transmitter. Acetyl CoA is a precursor used inside the terminal to build acetylcholine, not a product of its breakdown in the cleft. Phosphate is not part of the acetylcholine molecule at all.

cards.q: Is relaxation of skeletal muscle an active or a passive process?
cards.a: Active, because Ca2+ must be pumped uphill back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
options: Active, because Ca2+ must be pumped uphill back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Passive, because the elastic recoil of titin returns the sarcomere to length
Active, because ATP is used to pull tropomyosin back over the binding sites
Passive, because Ca2+ simply diffuses away from troponin
cards.explanation: Relaxation costs ATP, and a large share of a muscle's energy budget goes to SERCA. Ca2+ dissociates from troponin readily enough, but unless the cytosolic concentration is actively driven back down it simply rebinds. Elastic recoil helps return the muscle to resting length once crossbridges have released, but it is not what ends the activation, and no ATP is spent moving tropomyosin, which returns on its own once troponin C is empty.

cards.q: Which protein inside the sarcoplasmic reticulum lets the store accumulate a large total amount of Ca2+ without free luminal Ca2+ climbing too high?
cards.a: Calsequestrin.
options: Troponin C
Calsequestrin
Calmodulin
SERCA
cards.explanation: Calsequestrin binds Ca2+ with low affinity and high capacity inside the lumen, so most of the stored Ca2+ is bound rather than free, which keeps the gradient SERCA has to pump against manageable. Troponin C is the cytosolic sensor on the thin filament, and calmodulin is the Ca2+ binding protein of smooth muscle and many signaling pathways. SERCA is the pump that fills the store rather than the protein that buffers it.

cards.q: What ends the end plate potential after a single nerve impulse?
cards.a: Acetylcholinesterase destroys the transmitter, so the receptor channels close.
options: SERCA lowers cytosolic Ca2+ at the end plate
Acetylcholinesterase destroys the transmitter, so the receptor channels close
The receptor channels inactivate the way voltage gated Na+ channels do
Acetylcholine is pumped back into the terminal intact
cards.explanation: Ligand gated channels stay open as long as the ligand is present, so ending the end plate potential is a matter of removing acetylcholine, which the cleft enzyme does within a couple of milliseconds. SERCA works inside the fiber on Ca2+ and has nothing to do with the end plate. Nicotinic receptors do not have the fast voltage dependent inactivation that Na+ channels have, and it is choline, not intact transmitter, that is recovered by the terminal.

cards.q: Which step ends a contraction most slowly and therefore sets the duration of the relaxation phase?
cards.a: Pumping Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
options: Clearing acetylcholine from the synaptic cleft
Repolarizing the muscle action potential
Pumping Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Detaching the last myosin heads once Ca2+ has fallen
cards.explanation: Transmitter clearance and the action potential are over in a few milliseconds, while SERCA needs tens of milliseconds to drag cytosolic Ca2+ back down to resting level, so the Ca2+ decline is what the relaxation phase of a twitch is really tracking. Crossbridges detach quickly once Ca2+ is gone and are not the bottleneck. This is also why relaxation is the longest phase of a twitch and why summation is possible at all.

cards.q: A drug that specifically inhibits SERCA is applied to a muscle fiber. Predict the twitch.
cards.a: Force develops normally but relaxation is slowed or incomplete.
options: Force is reduced and relaxation is faster than normal
Force never develops, because the store cannot be refilled in time
Force develops normally but relaxation is slowed or incomplete
Force develops and relaxes normally, because release is unaffected
cards.explanation: For the first twitch the store is already loaded, so release and force development are normal, and the drug shows itself in the falling phase, where cytosolic Ca2+ lingers and the crossbridges keep cycling. Over repeated stimulation force would also fall as the store fails to refill, but the immediate and defining sign is slowed relaxation. Nothing about blocking a pump makes relaxation faster.

cards.q: Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase. What is the immediate effect at the junction?
cards.a: Acetylcholine lingers in the cleft, so the end plate potential is prolonged.
options: The nicotinic receptors are blocked, so the end plate potential shrinks
Acetylcholine release from the terminal increases
Acetylcholine lingers in the cleft, so the end plate potential is prolonged
The Ca2+ transient inside the fiber is prolonged directly
cards.explanation: The enzyme is the only fast route for clearing transmitter, so inhibiting it leaves acetylcholine free to rebind and hold receptor channels open past the normal couple of milliseconds. The resulting long end plate potential can drive several muscle action potentials from one nerve impulse, which is why small doses strengthen contraction in myasthenia gravis. Release from the nerve is unchanged, the receptors are not blocked, and the Ca2+ transient lengthens only as a downstream consequence of extra action potentials.

cards.q: A muscle fiber is cooled from 37 C to 25 C, slowing SERCA. Which part of the twitch changes most?
cards.a: The relaxation phase lengthens.
options: The contraction phase becomes steeper
Peak force doubles
The latent period disappears
The relaxation phase lengthens
cards.explanation: Relaxation time tracks how fast Ca2+ is cleared from the cytosol, so slowing the pump stretches that phase out most obviously. The latent period reflects excitation contraction coupling and cannot disappear, and the rise of force depends mainly on crossbridge attachment rather than on the pump. Cooling does not double peak force, although a longer Ca2+ transient can raise twitch force somewhat by keeping the filament activated longer.

cards.q: A working muscle runs low on ATP. Which failure explains why the muscle stiffens rather than going limp?
cards.a: SERCA cannot clear Ca2+ and myosin heads cannot detach.
options: Acetylcholinesterase cannot clear transmitter, so the fiber keeps firing
SERCA cannot clear Ca2+ and myosin heads cannot detach
The ryanodine receptors close, so Ca2+ stays in the store
Tropomyosin locks over the binding sites, holding the filaments together
cards.explanation: ATP is needed both to pump Ca2+ back into the store and to release myosin from actin, so its loss attacks relaxation from two directions at once and the muscle becomes rigid. Acetylcholinesterase does not require ATP to work. Closing the release channels or covering the binding sites would both leave the fiber relaxed rather than stiff, which is the opposite of what energy depletion produces.

cards.q: A muscle relaxes normally in every respect except that the end plate potential lasts much longer than usual. Which component has failed?
cards.a: Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft.
options: Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft
SERCA in the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane
Calsequestrin in the sarcoplasmic reticulum lumen
The ryanodine receptor in the terminal cisternae
cards.explanation: A prolonged end plate potential is a synaptic finding, and the only listed protein that works in the cleft is the enzyme that clears acetylcholine. All the other candidates operate on Ca2+ inside the fiber, and their failure would show up as an abnormal Ca2+ transient or abnormal relaxation of force, not as a longer electrical event at the end plate. Being able to place a defect from the measurement that is abnormal is the point of this comparison.

cards.q: A fiber is modified to express extra SERCA pumps. Predict the effect on its twitch.
cards.a: Relaxation is faster, because cytosolic Ca2+ falls sooner.
options: Relaxation is faster, because cytosolic Ca2+ falls sooner
Relaxation is slower, because more ATP is diverted from the crossbridges
The latent period is shorter, because the store is fuller
Peak force is higher, because more Ca2+ is released
cards.explanation: More pumps clear Ca2+ from the cytosol more quickly, so troponin empties sooner and the crossbridges shut down earlier, giving a briefer twitch. Fast twitch fibers really do have a higher density of SERCA than slow fibers for this reason. Pumping does consume ATP, but not at a rate that starves the crossbridges in a single twitch, and the number of pumps does not shorten excitation contraction coupling or raise the amount of Ca2+ released per impulse.

cards.q: A person is exposed to an irreversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. Trace the sequence from the enzyme failure to the weakness that follows the initial twitching.
cards.a: Acetylcholine accumulates, the end plate stays depolarized, and Na+ channels remain inactivated.
options: Acetylcholine accumulates, the end plate stays depolarized, and Na+ channels remain inactivated
Acetylcholine accumulates, the terminal runs out of vesicles, and release stops
